findings.title: isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted condition and wrong substring indices
findings.body: The new isAccessTokenId matcher contains `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. Two problems: (1) the condition is inverted — it returns false (no match) precisely when the grant shortcut equals the expected one, so the matcher only passes for tokens with the WRONG grant shortcut; (2) the indices are wrong — the encoded prefix is 6 chars with the grant shortcut at positions 4-5, so it should be substring(4, 6), not substring(3, 5) (which captures the 2nd token-type char plus the 1st grant char). As written, every updated assertion (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) will fail against correctly encoded token IDs, breaking the tests that use them.

findings.title: Constructor null-checks grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId
findings.body: In the AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth check is `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` — it re-checks grantType instead of rawTokenId. As a result, rawTokenId can be null, which later causes encodeTokenId() to produce token IDs ending in 'null' (string concatenation of a null rawTokenId) and getTokenContextFromTokenId('...:') to behave inconsistently. The check should be `Objects.requireNonNull(rawTokenId, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`.

findings.title: Public copy constructor Context(Context) removed from OAuth2GrantType.Context
findings.body: The PR deletes the public copy constructor `Context(Context context)` from OAuth2GrantType.Context and replaces it with a grantType field initialized in the main constructor. Any existing custom OAuth2GrantType provider (or internal caller) that wraps/decorates a context via `new Context(existingContext)` will fail to compile after upgrade. If the removal is intentional, note it as a breaking change; otherwise keep the copy constructor and have it also copy the grantType field.

findings.title: Lightweight-token flag derived from session context client, not the token's client
findings.body: initToken now calls DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext, which determines lightweight vs regular via AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session), reading `session.getContext().getClient()`. In flows where the context client differs from the client the token is issued for (e.g. token exchange sets the requester in the context), the encoded token-type flag can reflect the wrong client. Worth verifying and adding a test that a token issued for a lightweight-token client is encoded as 'lt' in these flows.
